Scrap windfall tax on oil and gas firms early, North Sea industry urges


Labour should replace levy in 2027 rather than 2030 as energy bills are poised to surge over the winter, says lobby group




The North Sea oil and gas industry has called on Labour to scrap the windfall tax on fossil fuel firms three years early, as Britain heads into a winter with energy bills expected to reach their highest level since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Offshore Energies UK (OEUK), the industry’s trade body, wants the tax replaced in 2027, rather than in 2030, with a narrower levy that only applies during price spikes.

OEUK is also pressing ministers to approve two big North Sea oil and gasfields, Rosebank and Jackdaw, as part of a call for looser regulation of the sector.







Mapped: the £150bn megaproject that aims to protect Britain from energy shocks

Read more
The current windfall tax, the energy profits levy, was introduced in 2022 after fossil fuel firms posted record profits when oil and gas prices spiked after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Its planned replacement, the oil and gas revenue levy, would charge a 35% tax on revenue only when prices rise above a set threshold.
Any decision to ease taxes on oil and gas producers would come before what is likely to be another winter of high energy prices due to the Iran war. Household energy bills are expected to climb to a three-year high this winter, while wholesale gas on Monday rose to 207p a therm, its highest point since the Russia-Ukraine crisis.
Companies including Shell and BP have already enjoyed huge profits in the months after the Iran war, which the campaign group Global Witness described as “cashing in on human misery”.


The OEUK chief executive, David Whitehouse, admitted that “from the consumer’s point of view … you can argue that it is a difficult time to make these arguments”.
However, he added that the new levy would “ensure that oil and gas companies pay high levels of tax when prices are high, but encourages investment”.

‘It’s really taking off’: hedge revival as farmers rediscover ancient tools


Grant applications in England surge as interest grows in habitat that captures carbon and helps reduce flood risk




The ancient craft of hedge laying is experiencing a strong revival as farmers use techniques that peaked in the 18th and 19th centuries to boost wildlife, capture carbon and help tackle flooding.
Hedge laying, which restores and revives mature hedges to keep them fresh, was among the four most popular categories of capital grants selected by farmers out of a total pot of £225m provided by the government this year to support practical environmental improvements on farms and across the countryside.

The 2,500 farmers across England who applied for grants to restore and maintain their mature hedgerows using a craft that dates back thousands of years, will – if the grants are approved – lay 1,300km (800 miles) of mature hedgerows, enough to stretch from Land’s End to Hadrian’s Wall and back.


View image in fullscreen
The craft of hedge laying fell out of favour after the second world war. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian
Megan Gimber, the key habitats officer for the People’s Trust for Endangered Species, said hedge laying was one of the most effective tools farmers had to respond to the climate crisis. “Hedge laying really stopped after the war, so it has been over a generation since it was a normal part of farm management and we have seen a huge decline in hedgerows as a result,” she said.


“These grants will give 1,300km of potentially ancient hedges a new lease of life, to help plug the gap, and it is fantastic that it is such a popular grant application.”
Mature, maintained hedgerows are a carbon sink, capturing more carbon in every hectare than forests. They support thousands of species, provide shade for livestock, reduce soil erosion and slow down, absorb and store vast amounts of rainwater to help reduce flooding.

If you think you have heard enough about the growing “super” El Niño, trust me, you are going to hear a lot more. What is happening in the equatorial Pacific is jaw-dropping and could well mark one of the biggest global weather upheavals in a millennium. It will spawn a string of weather catastrophes around our world in what remains of this year and in 2027, and there is no reason to think the UK will be immune.
To recap briefly, El Niño involves a heating of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific ocean. It happens every few years and is part of a natural cycle termed the El Niño southern oscillation, which switches between warm (El Niño) and cool (La Niña) phases. El Niños that see heating reach or exceed 2C are defined as “super” but this one, which is forecast to top-out at an astonishing 4C later this year, is so much bigger, the term “hyper” might be more appropriate.



El Niño is nothing new. Evidence for its existence extends back hundreds of millions of years and its ramifications have always been negative and disruptive. The difference today is that it is happening at a time when our world is heating more rapidly than ever before, and it is being supercharged as a result, leading to increasingly extreme weather.
Figuring out how much global heating alone is influencing El Niño is not straightforward, as its strength and other characteristics change naturally over time. Both El Niños and La Niñas, for example, have been steadily increasing in duration over the last 7,000 years. This is bad news in its own right, as it means the world’s weather is knocked out of kilter for even longer, but added to this, stronger El Niños are becoming more frequent as we continue to add CO2 to the atmosphere.
There is no straightforward correlation between El Niño’s strength and the magnitude of impacts in any given part of the planet. But given the unprecedented amount of extra heat being added to the atmosphere over the Pacific, it would be reasonable to expect the world to experience exceptionally hazardous weather over the course of the next several months.
How, then, is the UK likely to fare? The Met Office has already warned of the increased likelihood of a stormy and wet autumn and early winter, so it would be judicious to start preparing now for flooding on a serious – perhaps even epic – scale. Panama canal traffic to be cut again as drought from El Niño worsens


Latest daily reductions will further choke one of the world’s most important shipping lanes




The Panama canal plans to again cut maritime traffic due to worsening drought caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, further choking up one of the world’s most important shipping lanes.
The canal handles 5% of global maritime trade and about 40% of US container traffic; it is favoured by shippers because it usually reduces cost and transit times, especially for companies trading between China, Asia and the US.

From October, an average of 29.5 vessels will be allowed to transit daily – down 18% from 36 in August, according to a draft plan submitted to Panama’s parliament. In September, officials cut daily transits from 36 to 32 because of the drought.

The US and Israel’s war on Iran, and its disruption to the strait of Hormuz, has complicated logistics and added costs for shipping companies using the canal.


In August, with vessels waiting 10 days to enter the canal – the longest since May – a container ship reportedly paid about $4m (£3m) to jump the queue. Maritime companies usually pay a flat fee to reserve a slot to transit the canal, but a daily auction allows shipowners to place bids to skip the queue. Bid prices generally rise during high demand.
Shipping restrictions on the canal could yet worsen, with El Niño expected to peak later this year. The natural weather pattern that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns is forecast to be the strongest in four decades.
The 82km-long canal, connecting the Caribbean Sea to the Pacific Ocean, relies on fresh water from rivers pouring into Lake Gatun to operate its system of locks. In September, officials said the watershed had received lower than forecast rainfall.
The canal’s locks act like elevators, each filling with water to lift ships 26 metres (85 feet) from sea level to Lake Gatun and then back down to sea level on the other side.
If lake levels are no longer safe for the largest ships to pass, the Panama Canal Authority imposes restrictions for safety and to preserve water.


In 2023 the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low authorities cut daily transits from 38 to 22. Those restrictions led to a bottleneck of ships and sent companies scrambling to find alternative routes.

Back in April 2004, in the shadow of the previous European summer, I started work at Downing Street advising the British prime minister on climate change. The 2003 heatwave had killed an estimated 70,000 people across Europe. Many were older people, in homes and neighbourhoods ill-equipped for prolonged heat.
In May this year, I walked through Bordeaux with my 83-year-old mother-in-law in 38C heat. I saw how quickly heat changes the terms of ordinary life. Streets emptied. Shade became essential. The question was not simply the temperature, but whether people could work, sleep or remain safely at home.

That was the European spring. By summer, 42,000 hectares around Gironde and Arcachon surrounding the city had burned. France experienced its worst fires since 1949.

Europe’s warning is relevant to every Australian city.
Extreme heat is not merely uncomfortable weather. Between 2000 and 2018, extreme heat caused more deaths in Australia than all our bushfires, floods, storms and cyclones combined. Yet it remains under-recognised because it leaves little visible destruction and its effects are often recorded as heart, kidney or respiratory illness rather than heat itself.
And risk is not evenly shared. Older people, particularly those living alone, people with chronic illness, outdoor workers and people in poorly cooled homes are more exposed. As we age, our ability to sense heat, sweat effectively and regulate body temperature can diminish, while thirst can become a less reliable prompt. Staying hydrated must be a habit throughout a hot day, not an afterthought when work is finished.

articles.jina_text:
Down a short gravel track in a largely nondescript corner of Louisiana sits a gas processing facility, operated by a company whose chief executive is a major donor to Donald Trump. It may be the largest emitter of methane in the US.
The Energy Transfer site, located near the city of Shreveport, is named as the biggest single “super emitter” in new rankings of US oil and gas operations for the largest releases of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas that is rapidly overheating our planet, according to a new UCLA study, which is based on satellite data.

From January 2025 to June this year, the Shreveport facility spewed out methane at an average emission rate of 1.56 tonnes an hour, which is 15 times larger than the threshold defined in a Biden era program by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) as a super emitter event, according to the study. The Trump administration has put implementation of that program on hold but climate experts and advocates say reducing methane emissions is vital to limit the climate crisis.


The new rankings combine satellite data and public records to indicate a “potentially responsible operator” for each of the largest methane plumes, researchers at UCLA’s Emmett Institute say. Such a task can be complicated by a lack of official records naming sites with large methane emissions as well as ascertaining ownership of pollution coming from tight clusters of differing oil and gas leases.
Dallas-based Energy Transfer oversees a huge network of pipelines and processing properties in the US and is linked to four of the 15 sites highlighted in the new rankings, with the company responsible for 75 methane plumes in total over the study period – three times as much as the next operator. Other major corporate methane producers include Enterprise Products, Targa Resources and Enlink.

articles.jina_text:
Scientists have discovered nine new deep-sea sponge species off Alaska, offering new insights into the region’s largely unexplored marine biodiversity.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) announced the discovery on Thursday, saying the species were found in the Gulf of Alaska and the Aleutian Islands. The findings bring the total number of known sponge species in Alaska to 232.








Could this humble sea sponge clean up the world’s ports? 

Read more
The specimens were collected during Noaa Fisheries’ annual bottom-trawl surveys, which monitor groundfish and shellfish stocks. Researchers analyzed samples collected as far back as 2012, describing the new species in two recent scientific papers.
Often described as living water pumps, sponges are among Earth’s earliest multicellular animals, dating back more than 600m years. They filter seawater and help create habitats on the seafloor, despite having no brain or complex organs.
“Sponges are ecologically important,” said Sean Rooney, a Noaa fisheries biologist and co-author of the studies at the agency’s Alaska Fisheries Science Center. “They aren’t plants, but like trees in a forest, they provide complex structure along the seafloor that creates habitat and refuge for commercially important fish and crabs,” he added.
“Each time we find a new species, it opens up new doors … Deep water is hard to access, especially rocky places we can’t reach with bottom-trawl surveys. There are now more than 232 identified species of sponges in Alaska, and probably hundreds more that we don’t know about yet. The future in this field is exciting,” he continued.


View image in fullscreen
Biologists use guides to try to identify species of sponge and fish collected during a bottom-trawl survey. Photograph: Noaa Fisheries
Unlike most marine animals, which can be identified by visible traits such as fins and body shapes, sponges can be much harder to distinguish. Because they lack complex organs and other distinctive external features, scientists often rely on their microscopic skeletons and genetic material to identify them.


“DNA barcodes provide a quick genetic reference,” said Meredith Everett, a biologist at Noaa’s Northwest Fisheries Science Center. “Sponge DNA can be tricky because they filter-feed, and within their tissues we may find foreign DNA and biochemicals that inhibit testing. But despite the challenges, we successfully developed several new barcodes for Alaskan species,” she added.
Dense sponge communities are considered essential fish habitat by Noaa because they provide shelter that supports fish survival, growth and population recovery.
Sponges also produce chemicals to defend themselves against predators and competing organisms. Some of these compounds have shown promise for potential use in cancer treatments.

Just six months later, many liberal politicians began to go quiet on the issue themselves. As the 2026 midterms approach, that retreat is still shaping how some candidates talk about climate on the campaign trail.
The trend, known as “climate-hushing”, may reflect the limitations of Joe Biden’s climate policies, said Daniel Aldana Cohen, assistant sociology professor at the University of California, Berkeley, who studies climate politics and inequality. Green jobs and housing investments fell short of the climate movement’s desires, consumer incentives disproportionately benefited wealthier households, and Democrats struggled to effectively communicate their accomplishments. The president has since rolled back many Biden-era clean energy incentives and regulations.

I mean climate change is real, I've spent a 25-year career telling people it is real and documenting its impact on the region: Floods, dry spells, heatwaves and more. 
So why for many people does this year feel different - like climate change is finally "here" ?
Well in 2026, things have reached some sort of tipping point where we can start to see really obvious signs of change that had a huge impact on at least some of us.
A winter of endless rain, not just wet but never ending. 
Then the rain stopped and we were hurtling into drought. 
Then wave after wave of what felt like boiling heat.




Image source, West Midlands Fire Service
Image caption, 

Sheldon Country Park was one of the areas in the Midlands left scorched by fire 




We have had wildfires this year because things have been so dry for so long, the hot air has just sucked the moisture out of the landscape.
It leaves vegetation dead, dry and needing just a small spark to erupt into flame.
On Cannock Chase, I spent the day with Staffordshire County Council rangers, as they showed me around the black, scorched earth left behind after the fires that took place there. 
I saw pictures of dead adders along with cracked and burnt eggs belonging to ground-nesting birds.
It is not just wildlife affected by them - the ash from the fire is changing the chemistry of the soil itself. 
It is much more nutrient-rich and that is bad news for this rare lowland heathland, where the traditional plants prefer poorer quality soil.
Already green shoots of bracken are bursting through the blackened earth and that will crowd out the traditional heather, bilberry and cowberry.




Image source, Staffordshire Fire and Rescue Service

At its height, 15 crews tackled a blaze at Sherbrook Valley in Cannock Chase




The Met Office has a list of things climate change will make worse, including "increased risk of fires" but it also says the "habitable region of pests expands".
That is exactly what our farmers are seeing this year.
Bluetongue is an awful disease affecting cattle and sheep, leading to the death of lambs and calves. 
It is carried by infected midges and as the climate has warmed the region, infected midges have expanded north from Europe to now include the Midlands.

articles.jina_text:
Kilos and kilos of courgettes, cucumbers, tomatoes and salad leaves are ripe and ready for picking on a small Welsh farm in the rural county of Powys.
The haul being harvested by Tilly Gomersall is not just impressive after a difficult growing season hit by a record string of heatwaves and drought across all of Wales and most of England, but all the more remarkable given that 18 months ago the site was uncultivated pasture.

“Until now, I’ve just been turning the earth with my own power,” Gomersall says. “We’ve got a two-wheel tractor, but you do have to heft that around with your body quite a lot and we’re cultivating from pasture, so it’s really hard work.”
The site at Wern farm, near Newtown, is part of a scheme to encourage young growers to supply fresh produce to nearby towns and cities and boost domestic production in the face of increasing risks to national food supplies.
The 15-hectare (36-acre) site is divided into three plots, each with a holiday chalet where the growers live, as well as shared facilities including a barn and diesel generator, to cover any power not provided by the farm’s solar panels.
Gomersall’s farm, Cân y Pridd (Welsh for Song of the Soil), totals 4.9 hectares but she is now only growing on half a hectare, including in polytunnels, where she says she is “producing very big volumes for the scale”.


View image in fullscreen
Duncan Fisher, of Our Food Trust, which works to increase levels of homegrown produce. Photograph: Andrew Fox/The Guardian
She and her two neighbours are already providing fresh fruit and vegetables for the local community, through a veg box subscription service and at markets. In late July, they also started supplying fresh produce to Birmingham city council, where it is distributed to holiday clubs, giving disadvantaged children a taste of homegrown veg for perhaps the first time.


The Wern farm project was launched by Our Food Trust, a charity which is working to increase levels of homegrown produce and aims to tackle Britain’s food insecurity.
The UK depends on imports for about 40% of its food and has one of the lowest food self-sufficiency ratios among large western European countries, leaving it exposed to supply shocks prompted by the climate crisis, or other risks including geopolitical tensions and cyber-attacks.
Just 0.2% of land in Wales is used for horticulture, according to the charity, giving huge scope for expansion. “We have to produce a lot more food for the regional and local market and for our cities,” says Duncan Fisher, joint chief executive at the charity.
One way to do this is to remove barriers for young people who want to get into growing, Fisher says, but who often find themselves priced out of renting or buying land and a suitable home. “There are lots of well-trained and skilful growers who can’t find land to grow food on,” he says. “The price of land here is set by the market, by people who are not going to farm it.”

I have to confess that I rarely enjoy birding in montane cloud forests. The birds that live in these mountainous, cool and humid habitats are masters of disguise, usually passing themselves off as a leaf or other form of foliage. But if I want to see antpittas – elusive, ground-dwelling birds that rarely show themselves – then I have no choice.

So, on a cool, cloudy morning my guide, Juan Carlos Crespo, Fredy Ramón Castillo, a local ranger, and I are standing on a steep, muddy path close to Tapichalaca Lodge, 2,500 metres above sea level in the eastern Andes, waiting for the jocotoco antpitta to emerge from the undergrowth.
Fortunately, antpittas have a soft spot for food, especially the large, juicy earthworms Castillo has placed on a low branch nearby. He calls the bird, with increasingly loud and urgent shouts of “venga, venga!” (“come on, come on!”). The minutes tick by, until I begin to wonder if this is a lost cause.
Then, out of nowhere, a plump, thrush-sized bird with a chestnut back, grey front, black crown and white face-patch materialises just a few feet away. It proceeds to gulp down the earthworms as if it has not eaten for days.


View image in fullscreen
A jocotoco antpitta in the Tapichalaca reserve. Photograph: Javier Aznar González de Rueda

As they ascended a forest trail at dawn, they heard the sound of a bird in the far distance. As Ridgely recalled many years later, “It had this crazy call, sounding like an owl; but we had no idea what it was, and to be honest I never thought we would find out.”
Ridgely walked ahead of the group, and heard the sound much closer than before. He recorded the call and played it back to the mystery creature, which came crashing through the dense bamboo, right out into the open.
“I knew right away that this was something really special, which no one apart from the local people had ever seen – an entirely new species to science.” It was, in fact, one of the greatest ornithological breakthroughs of the late 20th century: while new species are sometimes discovered, they are rarely so large, noisy and so obviously different from other members of their family.

One manufacturer claims that there is an alternative option – shared solar panels.

articles.title: Andy Burnham ‘set to announce £200 energy bill cut’ – would you qualify?
articles.raw_content:
Andy Burnham is said to be exploring ways to bring down bills for those most in need (Picture: Lewis/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)



A £200 cut to energy bills could be on the cards for certain homes in the UK if the government goes ahead with a move it is reportedly preparing.

According to the Telegraph, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is investigating how subsidies can be targeted to households living in fuel poverty.

It comes as the war in Iran continues to push up global energy prices – with no signs of an end on the horizon.

At the beginning of next month, the price cap for the average UK household will rise by 4% to £1,723 per year.

Rising temperatures in the northern hemisphere are forcing populations of the insect further north, meaning Britain is now in the upper end of the “thermal limit” for certain species typically found in hotter countries, experts have said.



While warmer summers are leading to a rise in all species of mosquito in the UK, one in particular, Aedes aegypti, was found to be breeding in Britain for the first time this year.





Aedes aegypti carries the dengue, Zika and chikungunya viruses, although the UK Health Security Agency says the risk to the British population from these diseases is very low.

articles.jina_text:
A decision on approving the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea is to be delayed until later this autumn, with the Greens accusing Labour of hiding their position before the crucial Holborn and St Pancras byelection.
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, had been poised to give her recommendation to approve the Jackdaw field off the coast of Aberdeen next week.

However, multiple Whitehall sources say the decision is not expected to be made in the remaining few days before the House of Commons goes into recess on Tuesday for party conference season.
The delay means the announcement is unlikely to come before Holborn and St Pancras constituents vote in a high-profile byelection on 8 October, in which the Green party leader Zack Polanski is the candidate vying against Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali in Keir Starmer’s former seat.



Polanski has criticised the government over signals that it will press ahead with Jackdaw despite the hottest ever summer caused by the climate crisis.
After his selection, Polanski said Labour has “started the campaign with an act of dishonesty and betrayal”.
“They are clearly going to allow new drilling in the North Sea but want to keep it under wraps during a byelection where they know the public want tougher action on climate, not backsliding.
“Labour talks about change, but this is change for the worse. We have a climate crisis but Labour is taking the side of fossil fuel corporations, and the voters have a clear choice in this byelection between action on climate change or shortsighted rowing backwards.”
The delay also means Andy Burnham could avoid controversy over Jackdaw at the Labour party conference in Liverpool at the end of the month.
Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said delays in approving Jackdaw would mean it takes longer to increase UK domestic production in the North Sea.
In a letter to the prime minister published on social media, Bowie asked Burnham to confirm “suggestions that you are about to delay the decision on the Jackdaw gasfield until after the conference recess and Holborn and St Pancras byelection”.


He added: “If this is the case, it would be nothing short of you placing the interests of the Labour party before the interests of Great Britain.”
A separate decision is also pending on the Rosebank oilfield project.
Environmental campaigners have called for both projects to be abandoned, while the US president, Donald Trump, has urged the prime minister to open them.

Australia and Canada can learn from each other on climate if we separate action from declaration

Rosa Galvez





Climate integrity means being honest about the gap between emissions reduced on paper and emissions reduced in the atmosphere





Canada and Australia are both democracies built on abundant resources, extraordinary biodiversity and world-class science, with prosperity built substantially on mining, oil and gas. We are major fossil fuel exporters running an economic model incompatible with a stable climate, and living the consequences through worsening bushfires, floods and drought.
As I prepare for the Climate Integrity Summit in Sydney, I am struck less by the distance between our countries than by how much we have in common. We face the same defining question: how do we move beyond fossil fuels without sacrificing prosperity or nature?

Our political systems differ, but Australians are asking the same questions Canadians are: young people wanting action to match promises, Indigenous communities wanting real recognition of their rights, scientists warning about tipping points, businesses recognising that tomorrow’s economy will reward innovation over dependence on yesterday’s technology.







BoM forecasts strongest El Niño on record as research points to ‘alarming’ climate change influence

Read more
The challenge facing our countries is not technological. It is governance.
Canada and Australia have focused on reducing emissions from fossil fuels while avoiding the harder conversation about reducing our dependence on them. That distinction matters. It determines whether we are managing decline or genuinely transforming our economies. The world is already moving to renewable energy. Australia has started that shift, Canada is late to it. Expanding renewables while continuing to expand fossil fuels is not a transition, it is addition. Every extra tonne of greenhouse gas warms the planet, no matter how sophisticated our accounting becomes.
This debate is especially live in Australia now. Parliament is reviewing reforms to the Safeguard Mechanism, the country’s main industrial emissions framework. The central question: should major emitters meet their obligations by buying carbon offsets instead of cutting emissions on-site?

A new hurricane season record will be set this week as a historic and still strengthening El Niño stifles tropical development in the Atlantic.
To date, no hurricanes have formed in the basin, despite this week marking the peak of the season on average - and there's no sign of development in the near future.
It means a new record will be be set for the latest date in the satellite era (1960s onward) without an Atlantic hurricane forming.
Currently, the record is 11 September, set in 2002 and 2013.
In an average season, there would have been eight named tropical storms and three hurricanes by this point.
This year, however, there have only been five tropical storms: Arthur, Bertha, Cristobal, Dolly and Edouard.
With few indications that there will be any development in the next week, this will mean the longest stretch into in a season where no hurricane has formed in the modern satellite era.

In the eastern Pacific, where El Nino tends to strengthen hurricane activity, it has been fairly active season so far. 
There have been 13 named storms including five hurricanes, three of which were major.
This is close to the number that would typically develop in the whole of an average season.
The latest, major hurricane Lowell, hit Hawaii this week with damaging winds, flooding rain and high waves.



Super El Niño continues to strengthen




Forecasters predicted the Atlantic hurricane season would be quieter than average.
In May, the National Hurricane Center forecast a total of eight to 14 named storms, three to six of which would become hurricanes, including one to three major hurricanes.

While El Niño is the natural warming of the tropical Pacific, it can disrupt weather patterns around the globe.









As wind patterns shift during an El Niño, upper winds over the Atlantic increase and this leads to more wind shear, where wind changes rapidly with height.
Increased wind shear rips apart thunderstorms, preventing them from growing into tropical storms or hurricanes.

Environment Agency says talks under way about increasing prices for industrial users to try to reduce poor water management




Ministers are exploring making water more expensive for some users, in the face of severe supply shortages.
Despite the UK being a famously wet country, the precarious nature of the water supply has been made particularly acute this summer, with almost three-quarters of England and all of Wales in drought and 27 million people facing restrictions on their water use.

As the climate crisis worsens and demand for water increases, the Environment Agency has estimated that, without action, England’s water supply could be short by 5bn litres a day by 2055.
Helen Wakeham, the director of water at the Environment Agency, said that to plug this severe and growing gap, the value of water needed to increase.


“If someone wants an abstraction licence from the Environment Agency, what they pay for is the cost of producing the licence. They don’t pay anything towards the value of that water,” she said.
While millions of households in England are paying record levels for their water bills, Wakeham said that, for big industrial customers, the more water they used, the less they paid.
There was a “lively conversation” going on about whether we could “completely reframe the way we value and pay for water”.
“It’s the beginning of a conversation, but ministers have asked us to look at the value of water and how our abstraction licensing system works,” she said.
The Guardian recently revealed that less than 1% of businesses in England use more water than the daily needs of 10 million people. Some of these businesses, which include oil refineries, chemical plants and paper mills, face no requirements to cut their consumption.
With the government committed to make England an AI superpower, there are also questions about where water-hungry datacentres will get their resources from. Water UK, the body representing the UK water industry, warned the UK would not have enough water for future datacentres.
“The reason datacentres are water-hungry is because water is so cheap,” said Wakeham.


View image in fullscreen
An aerial view of the depleted Chew reservoir in Oldham, England, in August. Photograph: Brook Mitchell/Getty Images


Dr Doug Parr, Greenpeace UK’s chief scientist and policy adviser, said: “Every day, people are doing their bit to save water, but they are being hit with higher bills and hosepipe bans while big business gets cheap water access. From France to Turkey, Easyjet offers more than 630 routes, ferrying UK passengers to destinations across Europe and beyond.

The budget airline regularly announces new flights — just this summer, they revealed a new route to Pristina, the capital of Kosovo, as well as new flights from Bristol to Glasgow.

But now, the carrier has unveiled a domestic route that’s divided travellers.

Now available on the Easyjet website, you can book tickets between Manchester and Southampton.

Starting on December 4, just in time for Christmas, the trip covers around 170 miles (as the crow flies), each way.

It will be one of Easyjet’s shortest routes (not including those between islands), second only to the flight between Geneva and Milan Linate.

The cost to the environment

The announcement has left some eco-conscious customers asking why such a trip has been made available.

Aviation produces roughly 2.5% of the world’s carbon emissions, and is one of the most carbon-intensive forms of transport.

‘Nobody needs to fly between Manchester and Southampton,’ wrote Fiona Jade on X. ‘Literally nobody. There’s an hourly direct train!’

And user, Juo, wrote: ‘We’re in a climate crisis and airlines are doing s*** like this?’

As public air monitors disappear, federal rollbacks and state laws are making it harder than ever to know what’s in the air




As the US’s network for monitoring air pollution deteriorates, a Floodlight investigation has found that the chemical industry is going state-to-state to restrict one of the few options citizens have left for holding polluters accountable: low-cost air sensors.
Over the past two years, the non-profit investigative newsroom determined, lawmakers in Louisiana, Kentucky and Ohio have passed strikingly similar laws barring regulators from acting on air-quality data that communities collect themselves – unless it comes from Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-approved equipment that typically costs tens of thousands of dollars. Similar legislation has repeatedly been introduced in West Virginia.



View image in fullscreen
A California official calibrates rooftop air monitoring equipment used to track local air pollution. Photograph: Dave Clegern/Photo courtesy of the California Air Resources Board
In case after case, industry has made the same argument: community monitoring is not reliable enough for regulatory enforcement.


Yet when lawmakers in West Virginia offered a version of a bill that would have let regulators consider community data if it met manufacturer requirements, industry refused to back it.
The bill “essentially codifies what we are trying to prevent”, wrote Jeff Fritz, an official with the chemical giant Chemours, in an internal email. Bill Bissett of the West Virginia Manufacturers Association wrote that the compromise “neuters” the measure and left it “toothless”. That bill died, along with versions in 2025 and 2026.
Ohio slipped its monitor restriction into a budget bill last year, prompting a lawsuit from a group of plaintiffs including Donna Ballinger.
Ballinger has a low-cost monitor in her front yard in Middletown, Ohio, a few hundred feet from a steel plant that she says frequently sends black, white and gray particles on to her property. Fumes sometimes burn her eyes and throat, she said, and she often holds her nose when walking between her house and car.
“My fear is cancer,” she said.
The lawsuit she helped file alleges that the new rules make her monitor’s readings useless as evidence.
An early-warning system in decline


People have turned to low-cost sensors at a time when the public network they used to rely on is thinning out. Federal grants supporting that network have fallen more than 35% over the past two decades, adjusted for inflation, and the number of government air monitors nationwide has fallen by nearly half over the same period, according to EPA data.

Emissions of planet-heating methane and CO2 from natural sources are worsening the climate crisis, paper says




Rising global temperatures caused by the burning of fossil fuels are transforming the world’s forests, wetlands and tundra to the point they are releasing emissions that could further worsen global heating by as much as 30%, a new study has found.
As the world heats up, permafrost in the high latitudes is thawing, fiercer wildfires are burning in drying forests and wetlands and lakes are warming. All of these changes are themselves causing the release of planet-heating methane and carbon dioxide locked in trees and soils, therefore worsening the climate crisis, the paper states.

While scientists have long known of these “feedback loops” that amplify the impact of direct pollution from burning coal, oil and gas, the emissions from natural sources are largely unaccounted for in climate projections.
This additional heating is however significant, researchers found, with emissions from natural sources set to amplify global heating by 20% to 30% by the end of this century. This would add an estimated 0.2C to 0.4C to the global average temperature by this time, depending on the overall action taken by countries to combat the climate crisis.

Climate catastrophe is on our doorstep – yet Labour’s impending approval of further drilling will bring more pain for negligible gains





Pinch yourself, it’s happening again. Here is a Labour government spending a vast amount of political capital to earn tiny material gains while risking huge political losses. It occurred repeatedly under Keir Starmer, and now – with the impending decision to approve further gas and oil drilling in the North Sea – it is happening under Andy Burnham. You rack your brains to explain it, but no rational explanation comes.
Burnham is studiously cryptic about his reasons. His clearest statement to date goes as follows: “There is a resource there. When people are struggling, we can’t ignore that.” Does he mean that oil and gas workers are struggling? If so, this decision will be of little use to them. The Jackdaw gasfield, likely to be approved this week, will generate a grand total of 27 direct full-time jobs. The Rosebank oilfield, whose approval is likely to follow soon, will support 450 UK-based jobs during its lifetime. Yet the UK’s net zero economy directly employs 300,000 people, and a further 400,000 jobs are planned. The rest of the green economy employs more than 600,000. A just transition for fossil fuel workers, securing jobs in the green economy, is better for everyone.

The record was driven by a combination of climate change and the rising influence of El Niño, pushing heat into the atmosphere across the Pacific.
Temperatures for the month were 1.65C above pre-industrial levels - surpassing the critical 1.5C threshold agreed by countries to avoid the worst consequences of climate change.
While a single month above 1.5C does not mean it has been permanently crossed, it shows a trend towards breaching that limit.
The month also capped western Europe's warmest summer, with high temperatures pushing the season past the deadly heat of 2003.









Dr Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at Copernicus, described August as "a remarkable month in the global climate record", and its impacts had been "increasingly being felt by communities, economies and ecosystems across the world".
The combination of record air temperatures, record ocean heat and Europe's exceptional summer showed how climate change was now driving extremes across "both the atmosphere and the oceans", she said.



World's oceans hit highest temperature on record
UN climate chief Simon Stiell said the record clearly showed humanity's impact on the climate.
"The evidence is irrefutable: this is the spiralling price of humanity's fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fuelling," he said.
On top of the ongoing impact of the use of fossil fuels, the rise of a powerful El Niño is making matters worse, the researchers have said.
El Niño is a natural climate pattern in which a band of the eastern Pacific turns unusually warm, releasing vast amounts of stored ocean heat into the atmosphere and nudging global temperatures upwards for around a year.
The one currently being experienced is still strengthening and could become one of the most powerful on record, according to the Copernicus team.
The biggest impact of this natural phenomenon on global temperatures is expected to hit over the coming year, meaning the current run of records may have further to go.

In the first project of its kind, scientists are trying to answer if the future of Alaska’s streams and tundra may depend not on survival of the fittest but on how species adapt together

By Gloria Dickie




On Alaska’s North Slope, scientists tread carefully across clumps of tussock grasses toward a fast-flowing stream draining the imposing Brooks Range of ice and snow. Near Galbraith Creek, they string out a mist net for white-crowned sparrows. The birds have recently arrived from southerly latitudes, intent on feasting on the insects that will soon descend on the tundra like storm clouds.
The Arctic summer is short-lived, and sparrows have only a few weeks to establish territories, find mates, lay eggs and raise their chicks on a steady diet of bugs. From every ensnared bird, the scientists collect blood, feather and faecal samples to see what they are eating and how that changes over the summer.

One thing they want to know is whether the sparrows are consuming a lot of stream insects, such as stoneflies and mayflies, says Ian Shuman, a doctoral student in quantitative ecology at Columbia University. As willow shrubs claim new territory along the Arctic’s rivers and streams – a process scientists call “shrubification” – this could disrupt the life cycles of stoneflies and mayflies. If the songbirds also depend on aquatic insects to thrive, that might affect the sparrows’ prospects.
The tundra can feel immutable in its vastness. A sea of grass and moss extends as far as the eye can see. But above the Arctic Circle, change is happening faster than anywhere else on Earth. Snow is melting earlier in the spring, sending torrents of water downstream. By late summer, such early season deluges have given way to parched creek beds. The Arctic grayling – cold water fish in the salmon family – that swim between deep lake winter refuges and shallow summer spawning streams may become stranded in isolated pools. Their survival, too, rests on the mayflies and stoneflies.

Across the planet, global heating is reshuffling the order of life. Some species will prosper, while those that can’t adapt quickly enough will nosedive toward extinction. Evolution and adaptation have long been thought of as solitary endeavours – a survival of the fittest. But what if species could instead draw on their longstanding relationships not to succeed or fail alone, but to swiftly evolve and adapt together to climate breakdown, keeping whole ecosystems intact?

Reclaiming the streets: the architects clawing back Europe’s car-centric spaces


The European Prize for Urban Public Space’s shortlist highlights projects helping people cope with climate crisis




In the words of Joni Mitchell, the planners of many urban centres around the world “paved paradise and put up a parking lot”. The European Prize for Urban Public Space tries to show that cities don’t have to be locked in the automotive age for ever.
The prize’s latest shortlist, announced on Wednesday, highlights architectural projects that convert infrastructure for cars into spaces that help urban dwellers cope with the soaring temperatures of the climate crisis: roundabouts that have become splash pools, thoroughfares turned into green havens, and car parks into gardens.

Among the most eye-catching of the five finalists is Leopold Banchini’s Round About Baths in Logroño, northern Spain. The Swiss architect’s project sought to revive what he called a “lost space” on one of the main thoroughfares in the city, a concrete island with a broken fountain.


View image in fullscreen
Round About Baths attempted to reclaim a space that would normally be out-of-bounds for those without a motor vehicle. Photograph: Josema Cutillas
Inspired by 19th-century public baths, Banchini’s studio used uncut timber panels to build and place a simple structure directly on to the fountain. The existing water basin became a shallow pool, while cast-iron flower pots were repurposed as fire bowls that heat a steam room.
“We have given up so much public space to cars, and if you live in a city with kids you live in constant fear that they will be hit by a passing vehicle”, Banchini said. “It restricts our movement so much that we almost can’t see it anymore.”
Those trying to catch a glimpse of the roundabout baths in situ will be disappointed, however: Banchini’s structure was only erected for a week as part of the city’s Concéntrico architecture festival in June 2025 – inadvertently showing how difficult it is to permanently alter car-centric infrastructure.


View image in fullscreen
Leopold’s Banchini’s project in Logroño only stood for a week. Photograph: Josema Cutillas
“If we had built something more permanent, we would have had to engage with safety concerns”, said Banchini, noting that bathers were only able to access the roundabout via a zebra crossing on one side.
“The rules around car traffic are hard to modify, and any requests usually go all the way up to municipal authorities”, he added. “And politicians are really scared to touch anything with cars, because they fear it will cost them in votes.”

articles.raw_rss: A curious online row over this summer's heatwaves points to a wider - and worrying - shift in climate science.

articles.jina_text:
Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice shared a Telegraph article headlined: "Heatwaves caused by fall in pollution." He said cleaner air, rather than carbon dioxide, was behind higher temperatures and claimed the public had been "gaslit".
He was wrong to suggest that carbon dioxide is not the primary driver of global warming. But the science he was distorting is real - and much more interesting than his original claim.
The fossil fuels that we've been burning for more than a century produce two very different kinds of pollution. As is well known, carbon dioxide warms the Earth. But less well-known is sulphur pollution, which forms vast numbers of tiny particles in the air and reflects sunlight back into space, partly counteracting the warming effect of carbon.
Thanks to clean-air policies around the world - like the US's Acid Rain Program in the early 1990s, that reduced gas pollution from power plants - sulphur emissions are falling sharply while carbon dioxide emissions remain near record highs.
Scientists increasingly believe the loss of that cooling effect is slightly speeding up global warming.


The past three years were the three warmest ever recorded, and the Met Office says 2027 is "very likely" to replace 2024 as the warmest year on record.














And away from social media, the argument over Tice's tweet raised an even more interesting - and worrying - question. Is it possible that our planet is actually more sensitive to greenhouse gases than we imagined?
And if so, might the climate be changing more rapidly than we feared?
Dust on the greenhouse
Global temperatures jump around naturally from year to year. El Niño, for example, a natural warming of the Pacific Ocean, can temporarily push them higher. So a run of record hot years does not necessarily mean the underlying rate of global warming has increased.
Reto Knutti and his team at ETH Zurich have tried to strip out the effects of El Niño and other natural fluctuations to reveal the underlying trend.
"It's pretty clear that the rate of warming has accelerated," says Knutti, a professor of climate physics at the Swiss university and a former co-ordinating lead author for the IPCC - the UN-backed body that produces the world's most authoritative assessments of climate science.
A separate study published this year reached a similar conclusion after accounting for several major natural influences.
And it seems aerosols are playing a role.





Burning coal and oil releases sulphur dioxide, which forms tiny particles known as sulphate aerosols. These particles are bright and reflect some sunlight before it can reach and warm the planet's surface.

Stefania Di Bartolomeo was an early proponent of the environmental, social and governance (ESG) investing movement when she started Physis seven years ago. Her mission was to show just what companies were doing with the money investors gave them to fight climate change and encourage diversity – to bring transparency to sustainable investors. 
The Italian-born, Harvard-educated fund manager rode the wave of ESG in the early 2020s but then suffered, like many others, as President Donald Trump returned to the White House with a vow to stamp out climate change investing. Suddenly business was drying up and ESG was a banned word on Wall Street. Even worse for Di Bartolomeo, a few of her tech team staff from India were even stopped on the Harvard campus by ICE agents looking to expel immigrants.
The situation called for a turnaround, and so Di Bartolomeo embraced the AI movement and has spent the last year restructuring Physis into a data infrastructure business with a sustainability focus. A new website and platform are set to be launched this month, which importantly will allow the transparent data information the company had been selling to large investors to be available on a subscription level for smaller investors.




The new platform will also allow investors to build their own data bases to track the metrics of companies they invest in, including sustainable data but also other important financial, legal, and geographic information.
Physis, which was named after the Greek word for nature, has also partnered with Google on data and introduced an AI-powered Chatbot that allows users to let AI guide them through all of the analysis it offers on potential companies to invest in.

“Every analysis we do will tell you the pros and cons of where a company positions itself against competitors, but with a sustainability lens,” Di Bartolomeo says in an interview from her native Italy. “And for our subscriptions plans, instead of just institutions for $25,000 (£18,500) we can offer some access to small investors for as little as $99 (£73) a month.


“Before we focused on sustainability,” she adds. “Now we have a broader data capability – with sustainability, even (ESG) skeptics will see that they need the information.”
Like every financial services executive in the last few years, Di Bartolomeo has had to adapt to the AI boom and be competitive while still hanging on to part of the original mission. Moving beyond sustainability and adapting its core principles to AI represents a new strategy that Di Bartolomeo hopes will keep her company at the forefront of the new wave of data-focused investing.
